name: Tianeptine

lead: Tianeptine is an antidepressant approved in France and some other countries. It is not FDA-approved but has been sold in the US as a supplement.
It appears in looksmaxxing spaces as a mood or focus aid. No study has examined it for any appearance outcome.

paras: It acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist and appears to modulate glutamate signalling and neuroplasticity.
Documented risks include dependence, opioid-like withdrawal, overdose and adulterated products. The FDA has issued warnings and several US states have scheduled it.

lead: Tianeptine is an antidepressant sold under brand names such as Stablon and Coaxil in France and several other countries, where it is approved for major depressive disorder. It is not approved in the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia or by the US FDA.[1][2] It was developed in the 1960s and introduced in France in 1983.[1]

Its pharmacology differs from that of typical antidepressants. It acts as an agonist at the mu-opioid receptor and also appears to affect glutamate signalling and neuroplasticity.[1] At high doses it can produce opioid-like effects, and prolonged high-dose use has been associated with dependence and withdrawal.[1][2]

In the United States it has been sold online and in some retail outlets as a dietary supplement, and the FDA has issued warnings about recreational use and about products found to contain undeclared tianeptine.[1] On appearance-focused forums it is mentioned mainly in the context of mood and focus rather than looks, and no studies have examined it for any appearance outcome.
infobox: Oral (injection misuse reported in some countries)
Approved in France and some other countries; not FDA-approved; scheduled in several US states

paras: The approved use is major depressive disorder. Its reported efficacy in trials has been described as comparable to that of amitriptyline, imipramine and fluoxetine.[1] Other uses, including anxiety, irritable bowel syndrome, asthma and ADHD, are described as less well supported.[1]
Tianeptine has no recognised cosmetic or appearance use. Its presence on looksmaxxing forums relates to people discussing mood, motivation and stimulant side effects.

Compared with older tricyclic antidepressants, tianeptine is described as causing fewer cardiovascular, anticholinergic and sedative effects. Reported common effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, dry mouth, constipation and nausea, with rare reports of hepatitis and hypomania.[1]

Opioid-like euphoria at high doses, dependence and withdrawal have been documented, as have overdoses, often alongside other substances. Injection misuse reported in Russia has been associated with thrombosis and tissue necrosis.[1] Some US supplement products were found to be adulterated, for example with synthetic cannabinoids.[1]

Tianeptine was once described as a selective serotonin reuptake enhancer, but that description has been dropped; current descriptions emphasise mu-opioid agonism and modulation of glutamate receptors and BDNF.[1] Animal studies in the 1990s and 2000s found that tianeptine prevented stress-induced dendritic atrophy and impaired spatial memory in rodents and reduced stress-related hippocampal changes in tree shrews.[3][4]

In the United States tianeptine has been marketed as a supplement for mood or concentration and nicknamed "gas station heroin" in media coverage.[2][1] The FDA has warned about it, most recently in January 2024 according to Wikipedia, and several states including Michigan, Alabama, Ohio, Tennessee and Kentucky have scheduled it.[1]

Randomised trials for depression, mostly conducted in Europe, are summarised in reviews as showing efficacy comparable to standard antidepressants.[1][2] Registered trials include a completed phase 4 comparison with escitalopram in major depressive disorder (n=164)[5] and a terminated phase 4 trial in treatment-resistant depression (n=38).[6] No studies found for any appearance-related use.

timeline.event: Introduced in France as Stablon by Servier.[1]
